implementation_notes: Classic realization: an abstract AccessPolicy with a virtual decide method and a Guard template that consults it before forwarding to the resource. Virtual member functions provide the runtime dispatch and the policy is injected by reference, so policies remain swappable without recompiling the resource; the resource class holds no rule code. Prefer this form when rules can change at run time or live in another module; choose the std::function variant when a single predicate is enough, and the template variant when the policy is fixed per build and the virtual call overhead matters.
idiom_name: abstract AccessPolicy + Guard wrapper (runtime virtual dispatch)
pitfalls: A Guard holding a reference to a policy that is destroyed first is a dangling-reference bug; the policy must outlive the guard.
A base class without a virtual destructor makes deleting through AccessPolicy* undefined behaviour.
Caching decisions in a shared policy object without synchronisation is a data race; the decision method should be const and stateless.

variants.name: std::function / lambda policy predicate
variants.implementation_notes: The policy becomes a callable - std::function or a template functor - so rules are written as lambdas and composed (and-combine, or-combine) without a class hierarchy; the guard stores the predicate and applies it before forwarding. This is the lightest realization and the natural one for small rule sets or tests, at the cost of a possible allocation inside std::function and no place to hang policy metadata; choose the virtual interface when rules must be organised into families of policy objects, and the template parameter when the policy is a compile-time constant.
pitfalls: std::function may allocate and throws std::bad_function_call when empty; validate the predicate before installing the guard.
Lambdas that capture references (a policy store, a session) easily outlive their captures; capture by value or document the required lifetime.
variants.idiom_name: Guard over std::function<Decision(const SecurityContext&, Action, const Resource&)>

variants.name: Policy as class template parameter (compile time)
variants.implementation_notes: The policy is passed as a class template parameter, so the decision is selected at compile time, inlined and cannot be swapped at run time; useful where the rule set is fixed per build (an audit build, a read-only replica, generated per-tenant binaries) and cheap enough to check even in hot paths. The guard keeps the same shape - check before access, throw on deny - with no virtual call and no indirect function object. Choose a runtime form when operators must change rules without recompiling; keep this form only when the policy is genuinely constant and the extra template instantiations are acceptable.
pitfalls: Every policy change becomes a recompilation and a new binary; a compile-time policy loaded from configuration is a category error.
Instantiations multiply per policy and resource combination, growing compile time and binary size.
